tool.name: Polariscope and conoscope
tool.measures: the optic character (isotropic, anisotropic, aggregate) and the interference figure (uniaxial or biaxial)
tips: Turn the stone a full turn
Watch both the dark stone and the bright stone

steps.title: Polarized light
steps.text: Ordinary light vibrates in all planes. A polarizing filter only lets one plane of vibration through. With two crossed filters (the polarizer and the analyzer), no light gets through any more: you see black. A stone placed between the two can change that.

steps.title: Isotropic stone
steps.text: An isotropic stone (cubic or amorphous: garnet, spinel, glass) does not change the polarization of light. Between crossed filters, it stays dark when turned. Careful: some strongly strained isotropic stones show patches or a cross (anomalous double refraction).

steps.title: Anisotropic stone
steps.text: An anisotropic stone (uniaxial or biaxial) splits light into two rays. When turned a full turn, it lights up and goes dark four times, every 90°. This is the sign of a doubly refractive single crystal: quartz, corundum, beryl, topaz...

steps.title: Aggregate
steps.text: An aggregate is made of small crystals pointing in all directions (jade, chalcedony, lapis lazuli). It stays bright whatever the position. Summary: dark all the time = isotropic; four flashes = anisotropic; bright all the time = aggregate.

steps.title: The conoscope: uniaxial stone
steps.text: By adding a lens, the polariscope becomes a conoscope. You look at the stone under converging light, along the direction of the optic axis, and you see an interference figure. A uniaxial stone (a single optic axis) shows a black cross surrounded by coloured rings. If you turn the stone on itself, the cross does not move: the optic axis stays in front of the filters.

steps.title: Quartz: the bull's eye
steps.text: In quartz (amethyst, citrine, smoky quartz, prasiolite...), and only in quartz, the uniaxial figure has a particular centre: the cross does not clearly meet in the middle, and instead you see a round, pale spot. This is the bull's eye. It comes from the fact that quartz rotates the plane of polarized light along its axis. On a corundum or a tourmaline, the cross meets sharply: this is a way to recognize a quartz.

steps.title: Biaxial: the cross that opens
steps.text: A biaxial stone has two optic axes. Its figure shows two “eyes” surrounded by rings, crossed by dark bands. When you turn the stone, the black cross opens into two curved branches, which move apart towards the outside: they are sometimes called the “moustache”. A little further, the branches come back towards the centre and form a cross again. The cycle starts again every 90°.
